body:
How the Deccan was connected to the coast

The Deccan's prosperity depended partly on the movement of goods between inland production centres and coastal ports. Traders carried textiles, agricultural produce, metal goods, beads and other merchandise through valleys and mountain passes. The Western Ghats contained important routes linking the Deccan plateau with the western coast.

Naneghat was one such pass. Its association with a Satavahana royal inscription shows how important communication routes were to ruling families. Merchant movement also supported settlements and religious establishments along these routes.

Guilds and commercial organisation

Many craftspeople and merchants formed associations called shrenis, or guilds. Craft guilds could help members obtain raw materials, learn specialised work and distribute finished products. Merchant guilds helped organise exchange.

Some guilds also accepted deposits and used the money for commercial activity. Interest or other proceeds could support religious establishments. Thus, guilds could perform economic functions extending beyond the production of goods.

Bharuch as an international trading centre

Bharuch in Gujarat was known to Graeco-Roman traders as Barygaza. It stood near the mouth of the Narmada and was connected with inland western Indian trade routes. The ancient maritime account Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, as discussed in the textbook tradition, describes the port and its commerce.

Navigation into Barygaza was difficult because of the conditions in the gulf and estuary. Experienced local navigators helped incoming ships.

Goods described as importsGoods described as exports
Wine and fine clothCotton cloth and silk
Copper, tin and leadAgate and carnelian
Coral and gold or silver coinsIvory, perfumes and other products

Agate and carnelian are important semiprecious stones associated with the craft and trade traditions of western India. Their appearance among traded goods makes Bharuch especially relevant when studying ancient Gujarat's commercial connections.

Monsoon winds and Roman trade

Ships crossed the Arabian Sea and travelled between Indian ports, Arabia, East Africa and the Red Sea region. Sailors used the seasonal monsoon winds to make long voyages more efficiently. For example, the southwest monsoon assisted journeys from the western Indian Ocean towards the western coast of India.

Roman demand for Indian products, especially spices and luxury goods, contributed to this trade. Roman coins found in different parts of India provide evidence of exchange, but their presence does not mean that the Roman Empire exercised political control over those places.

Why political control must be distinguished from commercial contact

Satavahana rulers and Western Kshatrapa rulers contested territories and trade routes in western India. Bharuch remained part of wider commercial networks during this period, but it should not be described as a port held continuously by the Satavahanas.

Trade could pass through territories controlled by different rulers. A merchant's route, a king's military campaign and the political boundary of a kingdom are not necessarily the same.

Prelims focus

  • Barygaza: ancient name used by foreign traders for Bharuch in Gujarat.
  • Naneghat: an important Western Ghats pass associated with Satavahana history.
  • Shreni: an association of merchants or craftspeople.
  • Agate, carnelian, cotton and perfumes were among goods exported through Barygaza.
  • Trap: Roman coins indicate commercial connections, not Roman political rule in India.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, pp. 91–96, and Chapter 10, pp. 99–101; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 35–36; IGNOU, State and Society in South India: 200 BC to 300 AD, Unit 27, Section 27.8, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Trade links the Deccan through the Western Ghats to Bharuch and overseas markets; exports and imports connect territories contested by different rulers.
pictures.caption: Western Indian trade linked inland production, mountain passes, Gujarat and overseas markets.

title: Trade Routes, Ports and the Gujarat Connection

body:
Religious centres beside trade routes

The growth of trade and towns in the Satavahana period was accompanied by the development of Buddhist religious centres. Merchants, rulers, queens, officials and other donors contributed to monasteries and monuments. Some establishments stood near routes crossing the Western Ghats, where travellers could halt during long journeys.

Two important forms of Buddhist architecture were the chaitya and the vihara. They served different main purposes and are frequently confused.

Chaitya halls and viharas

A chaitya hall was a Buddhist worship or prayer hall, commonly containing a stupa. A vihara was primarily a monastery or residence for monks, usually organised around a hall with cells for living and study.

At Karle (Karla) in Maharashtra, an impressive rock-cut chaitya hall contains a stupa at the far end of the hall. Its architectural form helped provide a space for religious gathering and circumambulation.

At Nashik, Junnar and other western Deccan sites, rock-cut monasteries and halls were developed during this broad period. They are important examples of the connection between Buddhist institutions, donors and inland travel routes.

The Amaravati stupa

Amaravati in present-day Andhra Pradesh, near the lower Krishna region, was a major centre of Buddhist art. Its large stupa, or mahachaitya, became especially developed during the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, although activity at the site began earlier.

A stupa is a mound-like Buddhist sacred monument, often associated with relics. Worshippers could move around it along a pradakshinapatha, or circumambulatory path. Railings and sculpted slabs were important features of the Amaravati monument.

Amaravati sculpture is notable for elaborate narrative scenes depicting events from Buddhist traditions, including the life of the Buddha and Jataka stories. The figures often show movement, expressive gestures and complex arrangements.

In earlier phases of Buddhist art, the Buddha's presence was frequently represented through symbols rather than a human figure. Later phases of Amaravati art also included images of the Buddha. The monument's artistic development therefore occurred over time rather than in a single construction campaign.

Religious patronage was diverse

Satavahana rulers also supported Brahmanical rituals. The Naneghat inscription's references to Vedic sacrifices and the donations associated with Buddhist caves demonstrate that Brahmanical and Buddhist institutions both received patronage in the Deccan.

Prelims focus

  • Chaitya: a Buddhist worship hall, commonly containing a stupa.
  • Vihara: a Buddhist monastery or residential establishment.
  • Karle: a major rock-cut chaitya hall in Maharashtra.
  • Amaravati: an important Buddhist stupa centre in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
  • Amaravati's major sculptural development occurred in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE.
  • Trap: The Amaravati stupa should not be confused with the city of Amravati in Maharashtra.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, pp. 33–36; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 10, pp. 104–105, and Chapter 12, p. 123; IGNOU, History of Bharat: From Earliest Times to 700 CE, Unit 10, Section 10.6, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A chaitya worship hall has a stupa at the far end; a vihara residence has a hall with cells for monks. Both could be rock-cut.
pictures.caption: A chaitya was mainly a worship hall; a vihara was mainly a monastic residence.

pictures.alt: Stoneworkers use chisels and hammers to carve ornamental limestone slabs and railings beside the Amaravati stupa.
pictures.caption: Amaravati became a major centre of Buddhist stupa sculpture in the early centuries CE.

title: Buddhist Monuments and Art in the Deccan

body:
What the Sangam age means

The Sangam age refers to the early historical period of the Tamil country, conventionally dated from about the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE. The name comes from the Tamil word sangam, meaning an assembly or association, especially an association of poets.

According to literary tradition, Tamil poets assembled under the patronage of the Pandya rulers at Madurai. Accounts of multiple ancient Sangams belong to this tradition and should not be treated as a precisely dated sequence of historical institutions.

The surviving Sangam poems are especially valuable because they describe rulers and chiefs, warfare, generosity, farming, markets, ports, landscapes, personal relationships and social life. Their dates and compilation histories are not identical, so the entire collection should not be assumed to describe a single year or reign.

The main literary works

Tolkappiyam

Tolkappiyam is an early and important work on Tamil grammar and poetic conventions. It explains the organisation of Tamil expression and is closely associated with the literary traditions studied under the Sangam age.

Ettuthogai and Pattuppattu

Ettuthogai means the Eight Anthologies, collections of Tamil poems on different subjects. Pattuppattu means the Ten Idylls or ten longer poems. They are major groupings within early classical Tamil literature.

Some individual works are particularly useful for identifying places and political traditions:

  • Pathitrupathu: associated especially with accounts and praise of Chera rulers.
  • Pattinappalai: provides descriptions connected with the Chola port city of Puhar and its trade.
  • Maduraikanchi: describes features of Madurai and its urban life.

Silappatikaram and Manimekalai are important Tamil epics associated with the wider classical Tamil literary tradition. Their composition belongs to a later and less securely dated literary development; they should not simply be equated with the original collections of Sangam poems.

Akam and puram: the two broad poetic domains

Akam refers to the inner or personal sphere, particularly love, emotional relationships, separation and reunion. Puram concerns the public sphere, including kingship, warfare, heroism, generosity and social honour.

This distinction explains why the same body of Tamil literature can describe intimate relationships in some poems and political events in others. Poems also make extensive use of the natural landscape to express particular experiences and emotions.

Other kinds of evidence

Early Tamil history is also illuminated by inscriptions, coins and accounts written by visitors or traders from outside India. Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions show that an early form of the Brahmi script was used to write Tamil. Roman coins and imported objects demonstrate contacts with overseas trading networks.

Prelims focus

  • Sangam: an assembly or association of poets, traditionally linked with Madurai.
  • Tolkappiyam: an important early Tamil grammatical work.
  • Ettuthogai: Eight Anthologies; Pattuppattu: Ten Idylls.
  • Pathitrupathu: especially associated with Chera rulers.
  • Akam: personal emotions and love; puram: public life, war and generosity.
  • Trap: Tamil is a language; Tamil-Brahmi is a form of script used to write it.

[Sources: Tamil Nadu SCERT, Social Science, Class 6, Term III, History Unit 1, pp. 87–89, 2018 edition, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, pp. 89 and 96, and Chapter 10, p. 100; IGNOU, India: 200 BCE to 300 CE, Unit 4, Section 4.2, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A woman poet recites before a ruler and listeners in ancient Madurai, accompanied by Tamil poets, a harp player and a drummer.
pictures.caption: Tamil poetry preserves accounts of kings, occupations, towns and everyday life.

pictures.alt: Sangam poetry contrasts Akam’s personal love and emotions with Puram’s public themes of kingship, warfare, heroism, generosity and honour.
pictures.caption: Akam describes the personal sphere, while puram describes public life.

title: Sangam Literature and the Ancient Tamil Country

body:
The three ruling families of Tamilakam

The term muvendar refers to the 3 major crowned ruling families of the ancient Tamil country: the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. Their power depended on control of agricultural areas, important towns, coastal access, alliances and military success.

Each ruling family was associated with a characteristic region, principal centres and royal emblem. These associations are useful for distinguishing them in factual and matching questions.

Ruling family and principal regionMajor centreImportant portRoyal emblem
Chera; western Tamilakam and Kerala regionVanchi, traditionally associated with KarurMuziris and TondiBow and arrow
Chola; Kaveri valley and eastern coastUraiyurPuhar or KaveripattinamTiger
Pandya; southern TamilakamMaduraiKorkaiTwo fish

The Cheras and the western coast

The Cheras were associated with the western side of the ancient Tamil country, including parts of present-day Kerala and the Kongu region. Their commercial connections benefited from access to the Arabian Sea and the spice-producing areas of the western coast.

Muziris, also called Muchiri, was an important western port associated with overseas trade. Tondi was another port linked with the Cheras. Pathitrupathu provides literary information about Chera rulers.

Senguttuvan is a notable Chera ruler in Tamil literary tradition. The epic Silappatikaram associates him with the cult of Kannagi, also called Pattini. This is a literary association and should not be treated as a precisely dated account of every event described in the epic.

The Cholas and the Kaveri valley

The early Cholas were associated with the fertile Kaveri delta. Uraiyur, near present-day Tiruchirappalli, was an important inland political centre. Puhar, also called Kaveripattinam, was a major port on the eastern coast.

Karikala Chola is remembered in the literary tradition for military success, including the Battle of Venni, and for promoting agriculture. The historic stone diversion structure called Kallanai, or the Grand Anicut, across the Kaveri is traditionally attributed to him.

Kallanai helped divert river water towards cultivated areas. This demonstrates why irrigation mattered in the delta: more reliable access to water supported paddy cultivation and the agricultural wealth of the Chola region.

The Pandyas and the southern pearl trade

The Pandyas were centred on Madurai and the southern Tamil country. Their rulers were prominent patrons of Tamil poetry. The port of Korkai, near the southern coast, was associated with pearl fishing and maritime exchange.

Nedunchezhiyan is a notable Pandya ruler praised in Tamil literature. He is associated with victory at the Battle of Talaiyalanganam. The Pandyas' emblem of 2 fish should not be confused with the Chola tiger or the Chera bow and arrow.

Prelims focus

  • Chera: bow and arrow; Vanchi; ports including Muziris and Tondi.
  • Chola: tiger; Uraiyur; port of Puhar or Kaveripattinam.
  • Pandya: 2 fish; Madurai; port of Korkai.
  • Karikala Chola: Battle of Venni and traditional association with Kallanai.
  • Nedunchezhiyan: Pandya ruler associated with Talaiyalanganam.
  • Trap: The early Sangam Cholas and the much later imperial Cholas belong to different historical phases.

[Sources: Tamil Nadu SCERT, Social Science, Class 6, Term III, History Unit 1, pp. 88–91, 2018 edition, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 10, pp. 100–101; IGNOU, India: 200 BCE to 300 CE, Unit 4, Section 4.4, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Kallanai diverts Kaveri water to paddy fields, supporting Chola agricultural wealth; Puhar links the region to sea trade, while Uraiyur is inland.
pictures.caption: The Kaveri's water supported cultivation, while Puhar connected the Chola region with sea trade.
